changes.before: Replace the second lambda assignment with operation = nullptr. What prints?
changes.after: Store and replace a function-like operation with std::function.

before: std::function<int(int)> from <functional> stores a copyable callable taking an int and returning an int. It can hold different compatible lambda types behind one declared type. The empty [] capture list means this lambda uses no surrounding local variables.
auto is simpler when the concrete callable type need not change. std::function adds flexibility with possible overhead. Calling an empty std::function throws; check it in a condition before calling.
Assigning a new compatible lambda replaces the old target. Captures still obey their own lifetime rules; the wrapper does not make borrowed references safe.

Expected output or behavior: 4
6
. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Assign a named free function with the same signature instead of a lambda. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: A callable is something you can call like a function. std::function, from <functional>, can hold different compatible callables over time. Its stored callable must be copyable.
std::function<int(int)> accepts one int and returns an int. Both lambdas here match that shape. Their empty [] means they capture no nearby local variables.
if (operation) checks whether an operation is stored. Calling an empty std::function would throw an exception, so check when an empty value is possible.
The program prints 4, then 6 on the next line. The first operation adds one. The replacement multiplies by two.

Use auto when one lambda's own type is enough. std::function adds flexibility but can add extra work or storage. It also does not keep objects alive merely because a stored lambda captures references to them.
